Vitamin D, nutrient proxy and obesity

GLM, GAM and random-forest comparison

Main findings

We retain the logistic GLM: neither GAM nor RF improved held-out performance in the settings tested. Moderate/severe vitamin D deficiency and a higher nutrient proxy were associated with higher adjusted obesity odds. Evidence that the vitamin D association differed by diabetes status remained inconclusive (p = 0.274).

1 Scope

We assessed vitamin D and a nutrient proxy in relation to measured obesity, and whether the vitamin D association differed by diabetes status, among non-pregnant Australians aged 18–64 in the 2011–12 NNPAS. The main complete-case sample contained 2,616 participants, including 717 with obesity: 27.4% unweighted and 23.4% survey-weighted.

Obesity was measured BMI ≥30 kg/m²; vitamin D categories were adequate ≥50, mild deficiency 30–49 and moderate/severe deficiency <30 nmol/L.

The proxy is the equal-day mean of saturated/trans-fat plus added-sugar energy percentages: two valid recalls for 1,998 participants, otherwise Day 1 alone (618). It is not measured UPF or usual dietary intake. We retained vitamin D as categorical and adjusted for diabetes, numeric age and sex throughout. Requiring diabetes status excluded 9 additional records. Pregnancy was handled by exclusion, not a model term.

2 Why we use GLM, GAM and RF

Our main aim is to estimate interpretable associations. We also check whether the baseline’s simpler structure misses patterns that matter for prediction.

  • Logistic GLM: primary association model. Obesity is binary, so a logit model keeps predicted probabilities between 0 and 1 and gives interpretable adjusted odds ratios. Survey-based uncertainty accommodates the sampling design. Its main restriction here is that age and the proxy contribute linearly on the log-odds scale, not the probability scale. Survey GLM documentation.
  • Logistic GAM: targeted check of linearity. We replace the linear age and proxy terms with penalised smooths, allowing gradual nonlinear relationships while keeping separate, interpretable predictor contributions. This checks whether a constant log-odds slope is too restrictive. Our main GAM remains additive: it does not automatically discover interactions. GAM documentation.
  • Random forest: broader check of model structure. RF can capture nonlinearities, thresholds and interactions through successive splits without specifying their shapes beforehand. It therefore relaxes both the linearity restriction of our GLM and the additivity restriction retained by our main GAM. Averaging many randomised trees reduces reliance on an unstable single-tree fit. We use a probability forest so its predictions can be evaluated on the same scale as GLM/GAM. Breiman (2001), ranger documentation.

RF’s purpose is to ask whether that extra flexibility improves held-out prediction. Permutation importance and partial dependence help describe what it learned; neither supplies adjusted odds ratios or survey-adjusted significance tests. Better RF performance would motivate investigation of model structure, not establish a particular interaction. No improvement would not prove linearity or absence of interactions. We test the specific vitamin D–diabetes interaction separately.

3 Adjusted associations and nonlinearity

We fitted a survey-weighted logistic GLM and a logistic GAM with cubic smooths for the proxy and age (k = 6, REML). Both used the same sample and predictors, without a vitamin D–proxy interaction.

obese ~ diabetes + vitamin_d + upf_nutrient_proxy_pct10 + age + sex
obese ~ diabetes + vitamin_d + s(upf_nutrient_proxy_pct10,k=6,bs="cr") +
  s(age,k=6,bs="cr") + sex
Contrast Adjusted OR (95% CI) Raw p
Diabetes versus no diabetes 2.29 (1.17 to 4.45) 0.01603
Mild deficiency vs adequate 1.00 (0.66 to 1.49) 0.98099
Moderate/severe deficiency vs adequate 2.57 (1.29 to 5.14) 0.00829
Combined nutrient proxy: +10 energy percentage points 1.51 (1.28 to 1.78) < 0.001
Age: +10 years 1.52 (1.38 to 1.67) < 0.001
Female versus male 1.11 (0.84 to 1.47) 0.46487

Vitamin D was associated with obesity overall (Holm p = 0.027), driven by the moderate/severe contrast. The proxy association was positive (Holm p < 0.001). These are conditional odds ratios, not prevalence ratios or causal effects. Including diabetes estimates associations at the same diabetes status; it does not establish diabetes as a causal confounder.

The survey-adjusted restricted-cubic-spline test gave p = 0.159 jointly for nonlinearity; component raw p-values were 0.519 for the proxy and 0.102 for age. This tests a specified spline basis, not all possible departures from linearity.

4 Diagnostics and sensitivity

Check Finding
Collinearity GVIF^(1/(2df)) 1.004 to 1.059; weighted age-proxy correlation -0.128.
Influence: five separate single-record omissions Proxy OR 1.48 to 1.52; moderate/severe vitamin D OR 2.19 to 2.58.
Higher GAM basis: k = 10 Largest curve changes: proxy 0.50 pp, age 2.65 pp; vitamin D estimates 0.73 pp. 
Two valid dietary days only n = 1,998; proxy OR 1.67 (1.37 to 2.03); moderate/severe vitamin D OR 2.40 (0.98 to 5.86).

GVIF and Cook’s distance were auxiliary weighted-GLM diagnostics; omission sensitivities used survey refits and did not alter the primary sample. The proxy curve was stable to k, but the age curve was not fully settled. The two-day restriction changes both sample composition and measurement completeness; its vitamin D interval includes 1.

Day 1-only and two-day groups had similar weighted obesity prevalence (23.4% vs 23.3%), but moderate/severe deficiency differed (10.5% vs 5.7%). This does not establish random recall missingness.

5 Diabetes interaction

As a separate secondary analysis, we fitted obese ~ vitamin_d_binary * diabetes + upf_nutrient_proxy_pct10 + age + sex; the GAM smoothed the proxy and age. We combined the two deficiency categories (<50 nmol/L) because diabetic cells were sparse. We used the same 2,616 participants, including only 98 with diabetes. The odds-scale interaction remained inconclusive: GLM p = 0.274, GAM p = 0.247. This is not evidence of equivalence. Removing the proxy on the same sample gave p = 0.239.

Comparison OR / ratio of ORs (95% CI) Raw p
No diabetes 1.36 (0.97 to 1.89) 0.0711
Diabetes 0.55 (0.11 to 2.70) 0.4571
Ratio of odds ratios 0.41 (0.08 to 2.08) 0.2741

6 Predictive performance and RF interpretation

We used two repeats of household-grouped nested CV (5 outer × 3 inner folds), with identical participants and all five predictors, including diabetes, in GLM, GAM and RF. Tuning minimised weighted Brier score: GAM k ∈ {4, 6}; RF mtry ∈ {2, 4}, minimum node size ∈ {15, 40}, with 500 trees in outer fits. Scores were evaluated with biomedical weights per complete repeat, then averaged. RF case weights affected tree sampling, not survey-design inference.

Conditional survey-replicate intervals for fixed held-out predictions; retraining and tuning uncertainty excluded.
Model Brier (95% CI) Log loss (95% CI) AUC (95% CI)
Logistic 0.1691 (0.1568 to 0.1814) 0.5120 (0.4824 to 0.5416) 0.6733 (0.6438 to 0.7027)
GAM 0.1696 (0.1570 to 0.1822) 0.5132 (0.4825 to 0.5439) 0.6650 (0.6357 to 0.6943)
RF 0.1715 (0.1577 to 0.1852) 0.5201 (0.4850 to 0.5553) 0.6483 (0.6109 to 0.6857)
Null 0.1791 (0.1669 to 0.1912) 0.5437 (0.5166 to 0.5708) Not interpreted

GLM had the lowest observed Brier score and log loss, and the highest AUC. GAM was close (Brier difference 0.00055); RF performed worse in this comparison. GLM discrimination was modest (AUC 0.673). These comparisons do not establish definitive model superiority, clinical prediction utility or validity of every GLM assumption.

RF relied most on age, followed by the proxy and diabetes. Importance is the increase in held-out weighted Brier loss after uniform within-fold permutation (20 shuffles; original outcomes and recipient weights retained). It is predictive model reliance, not a significance test or causal effect.

7 Conclusion and next steps

We retain the diabetes-adjusted logistic model as our baseline: the evaluated GAM settings offered no predictive gain, and RF performed worse in this comparison. The k = 10 age sensitivity warrants expanding the inner GAM tuning grid in future validation; it was not part of this predictive comparison.

Next, assess available confounders, missing-data/recall sensitivity and independent validation. Cross-sectional associations, complete-case selection, limited dietary measurement and the small diabetic subgroup constrain inference. The nutrient proxy cannot identify a food-processing effect.

8 Supplement

Higher-k GAM and RF partial-dependence curves

RF curves use held-out-fold models; GLM/GAM association curves use full-sample fits. Correlated predictors can yield unsupported combinations. Local RF fluctuations are not validated thresholds.

Inference and reproducibility

We used the biomedical weight and 60 supplied replicates, with variance factor 59/60. GLM coefficient CIs use residual survey df; marginal probabilities use pointwise logit-transformed replicate CIs. GAM smoothness is re-estimated in each replicate with a fixed basis. Nonlinearity uses a separate four-knot restricted-cubic-spline Wald test, not default GAM p-values. Holm adjustment covers the two main exposure tests (and separately the two nonlinearity components). Prediction CIs condition on fixed OOF predictions; folds are not treated as independent observations.

# GLM coefficient CIs and p-values
b <- coef(result$model)
se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(result$model)))
df <- result$model$df.residual
# Match the table's age contrast (+10 years); proxy is already divided by 10.
multiplier <- ifelse(names(b)=="age",10,1)
b <- b*multiplier
se <- se*multiplier
OR_CI <- exp(cbind(OR=b,lower=b-qt(.975,df)*se,upper=b+qt(.975,df)*se))
p <- 2*pt(abs(b/se),df,lower.tail=FALSE)
survey::regTermTest(result$model,~vitamin_d,method="Wald")
survey::regTermTest(result$interaction$primary,~vitamin_d_binary:diabetes,method="Wald")
# Fixed-basis nonlinear terms and joint/component tests
q2_nonlinearity(result$main_design)$tests
# Marginal CIs: first row full-weight estimate; remaining rows replicate estimates
q2_replicate_ci(estimates,df=survey::degf(result$main_design),transform="logit")

All implementation is embedded below. No helper scripts, cached models or existing result files are required. No raw data are modified.

9 Reproducibility and complete code

This single Rmd contains the cleaning, models, diagnostics, confidence intervals, p-values and figures. Open it in RStudio and select Knit. A full knit refits every model and may take several minutes.

The only data inputs are AHSnpa11bp.csv and AHSnpa11bb.csv, normally in ../data/raw/ relative to this file. Set params$data_dir in the YAML header if they are elsewhere. Required packages are rmarkdown, data.table, survey, mgcv, ranger, ggplot2 and knitr, plus Pandoc (included with RStudio). Optional aggregate CSV/PNG exports are off by default; set export_results: true to write them to params$output_dir.

Use Code → Download Rmd for the complete source. The expandable sections below expose the calculations without repeating them in the narrative. The HTML embeds its figures and styling, but not participant records.
